title: MB2-03447
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Georgia. She is claiming refugee protection under section 961 and subsection 97(1)2 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (hereafter the IRPA).

From XXXX XXXX XXXX 2008, to XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, the claimant worked at the XXXX XXXX XXXX department XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of Georgia, in XXXX. As XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Her XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX, asked her to XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX who were members of the political opposition party. Because she refused to carry out this task, the claimant was threatened with arrest, as was her family.
In addition, the claimant was harassed by her co-workers and threatened with rape by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX because she refused to obey.
On XXXX XXXX, 2011, the claimant [translation] "left" her position and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, specifically for XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.
Subsequently, the claimant was advised to not speak with members of the political opposition party, and she was followed by police officers.
This is why, fearing for her life, the claimant left her country on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2012, to come to Canada to claim refugee protection.
The claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA. ANALYSIS Identity

The panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity, which she established by means of the documentary evidence on the record, notably a copy of her passport, the original of which was seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC).3 Credibility

When prompted to explain why she returned voluntarily to Georgia after her trip to England in XXXX 2012 instead of seeking refugee protection, the claimant stated [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, that was the first time I was threatened. I thought things would calm down. I did not want to leave Georgia. I went there (England) for one week because I thought they would forget me," adding that she wanted to return to Georgia for ten years to study there and help people, that she did not want to leave like she did, that she thought things would get better, but that upon her return things had worsened, which forced her to leave. Hesitant, she added [translation] "There is no limit when it comes to my person and the members of my family," leaving implied that she and her family were in danger.

The panel dismisses the claimant's explanations because it considers that these explanations do not explain to its satisfaction the reason she freely chose to return to the country where her life was supposedly in danger, when she was out of reach of the aggressors from whom she had received death and rape threats.

From the start of the hearing, when questioned as to why and since when she had feared for her life, the claimant stated [translation] "When I worked XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX I was given illegal tasks that I did not carry out because I did not want XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Because I did not carry out these tasks, they threatened to rape me and kill me." She added, "This started on XXXX XXXX, 2011. I resisted them for 10 months, and then they terminated me".

Furthermore, it should be noted that on page 4 of her response to question 31 of her Personal Information Form (PIF),4 the claimant states that [translation] "In 2011, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXthreatened to rape me if I did not carry out his orders. Several times I was subjected to sexual harassment by my co-workers and my superiors, going as far as violent attacks."

In the panel's opinion, this indeed demonstrates that the claimant reportedly was subjected to threats well before XXXX 2011, because she also stated that she received threats from her co-workers, therefore prior to her leaving her employment on XXXX XXXX, 2011.

Therefore the panel finds that the claimant's voluntary return to her country and the contradictions noted in her explanations indeed demonstrate that she is not telling the truth about the events she reportedly experienced in Georgia.

Moreover, with regard to the voluntary return, the panel is of the opinion that it is important to note that the case law has established that the behaviour of a claimant is an aspect that the panel may consider in the assessment of their credibility; the case law states specifically that a voluntary return is inconsistent with the existence of a subjective fear.5

In addition, to support her refugee protection claim, the claimant filed her employment record.6 At the hearing, the panel asked the interpreter to translate from this record the line written under the item dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. It was indicated that the claimant was relieved of her duties at her request, in other words, that she resigned and was not terminated as she alleges.

When confronted with this alternative version of the facts, having stated that she was terminated because she refused to carry out orders from her superior officers, the claimant testified [translation] "I did not ask to be relieved of my duties. They wrote that so that I could not lodge a complaint. In the morning, they denied my access (to the office) and they told me that I was relieved of my duties." Seemingly embarrassed, she added, "They wrote that, like that, at my request, because I cannot go before the courts so that I may return to work there. That is why they use that form (of writing)."

The panel dismisses the allegations of the claimant because it is of the opinion that her allegations do not explain to its satisfaction the contradiction raised. Furthermore, on page 3 of her response to question 31 of her PIF, the claimant clearly states: [translation] I had to leave my job because I was very scared. On XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011, I left my position, but I immediately began working as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX [Emphasis added]

Also, the claimant described the agent of persecution as powerful individuals. When questioned as to how she managed to leave the airport when these individuals were reportedly looking for her, the claimant answered [translation] "I had no criminal record. They could not arrest me. According to the law in Georgia, one cannot be arrested at the border."

The panel dismisses the claimant's explanations because it finds it implausible that the authorities in Georgia would be unable to arrest one of its citizens at the border. Furthermore, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX testimony, individuals who are unscrupulous in fabricating false charges against innocent people and they told her they would arrest her. Internal flight alternative (IFA)

Moreover, when questioned as to whether she could go and live in complete safety in XXXX, the claimant stated [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX; it is 200 kilometres from XXXX. I know that Canada is a democratic country where my rights will be protected and where I will be safe."

The panel dismisses the claimant's explanations, which it finds not credible and non-satisfactory, because the fact that Canada is a democratic country and that XXXX is a city XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX do not explain in a satisfactory manner why she could not go live in this city.

Furthermore, when prompted to explain why she could not go live in a city further away from XXXX, such as XXXX, the claimant stated [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. It would be easy to find me and give orders by telephone. Here, I have come to be very far from them, so that I am out of their reach."

The panel dismisses the claimant's explanations, which it finds not credible because now the claimant has returned to her first version of the facts in stating that these individuals are very powerful and that they are capable of easily fabricating false charges, whereas earlier she testified that they were unable to stop her from clearing airport security because she did not have a criminal record and they did not have authority at the border. Therefore, the panel cannot help but note that the claimant used the argument of powerful individuals only when it was convenient to her.
After analyzing the testimonial and documentary evidence, the panel determines that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection."
Therefore, the panel rejects her refugee protection claim.

Jean-Guy Jam Me Jean-Guy Jam March 19, 2014 2014 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, (a) is outside the reach of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of each of those countries; or (b) not having a country of nationality, is outside the country of their former habitual residence and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to return to that country. 2 97(1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care. 3 Exhibit A-2: Immigration documents. 4 Exhibit P-1: Claimant's Personal Information Form. 5 Gonzales v.
